title: Check if two strings are anagrams (same letters in different order, e.g., "listen" and "silent") — sort both and compare, or use character frequency count.
shortTitle: Check if two strings are anagrams

s1_definition.profdef: Two strings are anagrams if they contain exactly the same characters with the same frequencies, just in a different order. The optimal check builds a frequency count of characters, incrementing for the first string and decrementing for the second; if all counts end at zero they are anagrams. This is O(n) time and O(1) space for a fixed alphabet. The simpler alternative sorts both strings and compares, which is O(n log n).
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India wants to detect duplicate payee names entered with letters shuffled, a trick sometimes used in fraud. "Rajesh" and "Hersja" use the same letters rearranged. A clerk tallies each letter of the first name, then crosses one off for each letter of the second name; if every tally cancels to zero, the names use identical letters.
s1_definition.oneliner: Anagrams have identical character frequencies — count up for one string, count down for the other, and check everything cancels to zero.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two strings are anagrams if they contain exactly the same characters with the same frequencies, just in a different order. The optimal check builds a frequency count of characters, incrementing for the first string and decrementing for the second; if all counts end at zero they are anagrams. This is O(n) time and O(1) space for a fixed alphabet. The simpler alternative sorts both strings and compares, which is O(n log n).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India wants to detect duplicate payee names entered with letters shuffled, a trick sometimes used in fraud. "Rajesh" and "Hersja" use the same letters rearranged. A clerk tallies each letter of the first name, then crosses one off for each letter of the second name; if every tally cancels to zero, the names use identical letters.

**One line to remember:** Anagrams have identical character frequencies — count up for one string, count down for the other, and check everything cancels to zero.

sections.s2_technical:
The frequency-count method is the efficient one. You first check the lengths: if they differ, they cannot be anagrams, so return false immediately. Otherwise you keep a count per character. You loop over the first string incrementing the count for each character, and over the second string decrementing. If any count goes negative or ends non-zero, the strings are not anagrams. In practice you can use an `int[26]` for lowercase letters or a `HashMap<Character,Integer>` for arbitrary characters.

The sort-and-compare method is simpler to write: convert both to char arrays, sort them, and compare. If the sorted sequences are equal, the strings are anagrams. This is correct and easy to reason about, but it costs O(n log n) because of the sort, versus O(n) for the frequency count.

Normalisation matters: usually you lowercase and ignore spaces so "Listen" and "Silent" count as anagrams. The frequency approach uses O(1) space when the alphabet is fixed at 26 letters, because the counter array size does not grow with input length. A senior nuance is that for Unicode text beyond ASCII you would use a HashMap keyed by code point rather than a fixed 26-slot array.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a fraud check: a fraudster sometimes re-enters an existing payee name with the letters shuffled to slip past an exact-match filter. The system must detect when two names are anagrams of each other. This is exactly how the anagram check works — compare character frequencies.

Problem 2 — Names come in mixed case and may contain spaces, but "Priya Sharma" and "Ayirp Amrahs" should still be flagged. This is exactly why we lowercase and strip spaces before counting characters.

The code has a `FraudNameChecker` class with an `areAnagrams` method using the frequency-count approach. The demo checks a few name pairs.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: `"Rajesh"` and `"Hersja"`.

Step 1 — Normalise both to lowercase without spaces: `"rajesh"` and `"hersja"`. Lengths are both 6, so we proceed.

Step 2 — Count up over `"rajesh"`: r=1, a=1, j=1, e=1, s=1, h=1.

Step 3 — Count down over `"hersja"`: h goes to 0, e goes to 0, r goes to 0, s goes to 0, j goes to 0, a goes to 0. No count ever goes negative.

Step 4 — Since lengths matched and nothing went negative, every count is zero, so return true.

Step 5 — For `"Rajesh"` versus `"Priya"`, the lengths differ (6 versus 5), so it returns false at the quick-reject step.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] 'Priya Sharma' vs 'Ayirp Amrahs' anagram? true
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] 'Rajesh' vs 'Hersja' anagram? true
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] 'Rajesh' vs 'Priya' anagram? false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Input: "Rajesh", "Hersja"
    │
    ▼
  FraudNameChecker.areAnagrams()
    │ normalise → "rajesh", "hersja"
    │ length 6 == 6
    │ count up:   {r:1,a:1,j:1,e:1,s:1,h:1}
    │ count down: h→0 e→0 r→0 s→0 j→0 a→0  (never negative)
    ▼
  all zero → return true

  "Rajesh"(6) vs "Priya"(5): length mismatch → false (quick reject)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Two strings are anagrams when they contain exactly the same characters with the same frequencies, only in a different order. The optimal way I check this is a frequency count. I first compare lengths, because strings of different length can never be anagrams, which is a cheap early reject. Then I build a count of characters, adding one for each character of the first string and subtracting one for each character of the second string. If any count goes negative or ends non-zero, they are not anagrams; if everything cancels to zero, they are. This is linear time, and constant space when the alphabet is fixed.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used anagram detection in a fraud check. A fraudster sometimes re-enters an existing payee name with the letters shuffled to slip past an exact-match filter, so I compare a new payee name against known names to see if one is an anagram of another and flag it for manual review. Before comparing I normalise the names by lowercasing them and removing spaces, so a name like Priya Sharma matches its shuffled form regardless of case or spacing.

I always mention the alternative of sorting both strings and comparing them, which is simpler to write but costs order n log n because of the sort, compared with linear time for the frequency count. For a fraud service that checks every incoming payment against many stored names, the linear frequency approach is the better choice. For text beyond basic ASCII I would key the counts by code point in a HashMap rather than using a fixed array of twenty-six slots.
